title: rename() rejects a case-only title change as a name collision: the next !== path self-collision guard is case-sensitive while getAbstractFileByPath is not (Notes -> notes throws 'A fragment with that title already exists')
description:
## Summary

`rename()` rejects a legitimate **case-only** title change as a name collision, telling the
user "A fragment with that title already exists." when the colliding file is the very fragment
being renamed.

The self-collision guard in `rename()` compares paths with a **case-sensitive** string
inequality, but the existence check it guards runs through `vault.getAbstractFileByPath()`,
which Obsidian resolves **case-insensitively**. The two never agree, so changing
`Notes.md` -> `notes.md` falls into the collision branch and throws.

## Root cause

`src/library.ts`, `rename()`:

```ts
async rename(path: string, title: string): Promise<string> {
  const file = this.file(path);
  const safe = title.trim().replace(/[\\/:*?"<>|]/g, "-");
  if (!safe) throw new Error("Enter a title.");
  const next = `${file.parent?.path}/${safe}.md`;
  if (next === this.scratchpadPath())
    throw new Error("That title is reserved for the scratchpad.");
  if (next !== path && this.app.vault.getAbstractFileByPath(next))   // <-- the mismatch
    throw new Error("A fragment with that title already exists.");
  await run(() => this.app.fileManager.renameFile(file, next));
  ...
}
```

`next !== path` is a plain JavaScript string comparison and is case-sensitive. For a
case-only rename it evaluates to `true`, so the self-collision is *not* excluded and the
existence check runs. Obsidian's `Vault.getAbstractFileByPath()` resolves paths
case-insensitively, so that lookup returns the **same file** and the guard throws.

Net effect: the guard is trying to say "don't collide with yourself", but the only test it
uses to recognise "yourself" is stricter than the test it uses to detect a collision.

The same shape appears in `move()`:

```ts
const next = `${folder}/${file.name}`;
if (next !== path && this.app.vault.getAbstractFileByPath(next))
  throw new Error("A fragment with that title already exists there.");
```

## Impact

A one-character, entirely legitimate edit is refused with a message that names a conflict
that does not exist. The fragment is left unchanged, so the user cannot retitle
`Notes.md` to `notes.md` (or `Work.md` to `work.md`, `Api.md` to `api.md`, ...) at all -
the class of edit users make most often when fixing capitalisation.

From the UI (`src/app.tsx`, `rename` in `useController`) the failure surfaces as:

```tsx
const rename = async (value: string): Promise<void> => {
  if (!selectedItem || value.trim() === selectedItem.title) return;
  try {
    await save(false);
    setSelected(await library.rename(selectedItem.path, value));
  } catch (error) {
    errorNotice(error as Error);          // <-- Notice: "A fragment with that title already exists."
  }
};
```

so the user is told another fragment is in the way, which is wrong and sends them looking
for a conflict that does not exist. The title input keeps the rejected text (that part is
already tracked separately as `fragments-d2h`); the defect here is that the rename is
rejected at all.

This is distinct from `fragments-b99` (sanitised filename vs. raw stored title) and from
`fragments-89q` (a doubled `.md` extension): both of those are about the *text* of the
title, whereas this is purely about the collision guard's case handling.

## Steps to Reproduce

Observed by executing the real `src/library.ts` against a vault stub whose
`getAbstractFileByPath` resolves case-insensitively, as Obsidian documents.

1. Create a fragment titled `Notes` (`Fragments/Notes.md`).
2. Edit its title to `notes` (lowercase) and blur the title field.
3. **Expected:** the fragment is renamed to `notes.md` and the title becomes `notes`.
4. **Actual:** a Notice reads "A fragment with that title already exists." and nothing
   changes. No other fragment is named `notes`, and the file being renamed *is* the only
   match.

## Evidence

```
$ node /tmp/bl-scratch/rename-case.mjs
before: Fragments/Notes.md (title=Notes), Fragments/Other.md (title=Other)

--- rename 'Notes' -> 'notes' (case-only change, same file) ---
  THREW: A fragment with that title already exists.

--- rename 'Other' -> 'other' ---
  THREW: A fragment with that title already exists.

--- control: rename 'Other' -> 'Brand New' (genuine change) ---
  OK -> Fragments/Brand New.md
```

The control proves the harness is not simply failing every rename: a real change succeeds and
only the case-only changes are refused.

Harness detail, stated explicitly rather than assumed: the defect is the **mismatch** between
a case-sensitive `next !== path` guard and a case-insensitive existence lookup. The stub
models the lookup as case-insensitive to match documented Obsidian behaviour
(`Vault.getAbstractFileByPath`); the case-sensitive string comparison in `rename()` is read
directly from the real source. Observed, not inferred, is the result: both case-only renames
throw, and the guard is the only code on that path that can throw it.

## Affected code

- `src/library.ts` - `rename()` collision guard (`next !== path` + `getAbstractFileByPath`)
- `src/library.ts` - `move()` has the identical guard shape
- `src/app.tsx` - `rename` in `useController` surfaces the wrong error via `errorNotice`

title: move() refuses a legitimate move on a filename clash but blames a nonexistent title
description:
## Summary

`FragmentLibrary.move()` decides whether a move is allowed by testing the **destination path**, but
the error it raises claims the blocker is a **title**. Two fragments with completely different
titles that merely share a *filename* therefore block each other: moving one into the other's
collection is refused with "A fragment with that title already exists there." even though no
fragment with that title exists anywhere in the vault.

The `move` control in the Collection `<select>` is a documented feature ("The app supports search
across titles, tags, collections, and note bodies; ... rename; move; and trash"), and this makes it
unusable between any two collections that contain same-named notes — with an error message that
names a nonexistent title, sending the user to look for a fragment that does not exist.

## Root cause

`move` never looks at titles. It composes the destination from the collection plus the file's
**current name**, and guards on that path:

```ts
// src/library.ts — move
async move(path: string, collection: string): Promise<string> {
    const file = this.file(path);
    const folder = collection ? `${this.folder()}/${collection}` : this.folder();
    await this.ensureFolder(folder);
    const next = `${folder}/${file.name}`;                          // <-- filename, not title
    if (next === this.scratchpadPath())
      throw new Error("That filename is reserved for the scratchpad.");
    if (next !== path && this.app.vault.getAbstractFileByPath(next))
      throw new Error("A fragment with that title already exists there.");   // <-- claims "title"
```

Two things are wrong and they compound:

1. **The guard is a filename check.** `file.name` is carried over unchanged by the move, so the
   only way it can collide is if the destination already holds a note with the same filename. The
   fragments' `title` frontmatter is never consulted, because a move does not change it.
2. **The message asserts a title conflict.** Note that the adjacent guard two lines above it
   correctly says *"That **filename** is reserved for the scratchpad"* — so the function already
   knows how to describe a filename-level clash, and the copy is inconsistent within itself.

The user is therefore told a title conflict exists, looks for a fragment with that title, finds
none, and has no way to satisfy the check: the blocker is an unrelated note in the target collection
whose name they can only change by renaming the fragment *first*.

## Trigger

1. Have two notes with the same filename in different collections, with distinct titles. This is
   ordinary vault content — same-named notes per project folder is a common layout — and Fragments
   itself creates `Untitled fragment.md`, `Untitled fragment 2.md`, ... in every collection, so two
   collections that each received a snippet from **New Snippet** will collide on the second one.
2. Select one of them, open the Collection `<select>`, and choose the collection holding the other.

## Impact

- **A documented feature is blocked**, with no workaround inside the app short of renaming the
  fragment before moving it — which itself hits the `rename` guard for any target that is taken.
- **The error is factually false.** It names a title that exists nowhere in the vault, so the user's
  natural debugging step (find the conflicting title) cannot succeed.
- Reachable from the plugin's own output: create snippets in two collections and the second create
  lands on a filename the first already used.

## Expected vs actual

- **Expected:** either the move succeeds, or the error names the actual obstacle — a note named
  `dup.md` already exists in `Archive`.
- **Actual:** the move is refused and the error attributes it to a title conflict that does not
  exist.

## Evidence

Real `src/library.ts` bundled from `src/` with esbuild and driven by an in-memory vault. No React,
no timing, no concurrency.

Vault:

- `Fragments/Work/dup.md` — `title: "Onboarding checklist"`
- `Fragments/Archive/dup.md` — `title: "Quarterly budget"`

```
titles in the vault                "Onboarding checklist", "Quarterly budget"
filenames in the vault             dup.md, dup.md
any fragment titled 'dup'?         NO
move('Onboarding checklist' -> Archive)   REJECTED -> A fragment with that title already exists there.
vault truth after                  ["Fragments/Work/dup.md","Fragments/Archive/dup.md"]
no fragment named 'dup' exists     confirmed
```

The two titles are disjoint, so the message describes a conflict that cannot exist. The files are
untouched, confirming the refusal is the guard and not a vault failure.

**Control** — a fragment whose filename is unique in the destination moves normally, which isolates
the cause to the filename check rather than to `move` or `ensureFolder`:

```
CONTROL: move('Fragments/Work/unique.md' -> Archive)   ok -> Fragments/Archive/unique.md
```

## Where to fix

`src/library.ts`, `move`. The check itself is sound — a destination filename genuinely must be
unique — so the defect is the message and the missing guidance. At minimum, say what is actually
blocking, and name the file:

```ts
if (next !== path && this.app.vault.getAbstractFileByPath(next))
  throw new Error(`“${file.name}” already exists in ${collection || "the library root"}.`);
```

Better, make the move recoverable: auto-derive a free name in the destination
(`dup 2.md`, as `create()` already does) so a filename clash never blocks a move, and only surface an
error when a *title* conflict genuinely exists. A regression test asserting that two same-named,
differently-titled fragments in different collections can be moved, and that any refusal mentions
the filename, would pin this down.

## Related but distinct

- `fragments-b99` — `rename()` sanitises the filename but stores the raw title, so the guard there
  tests a *sanitised* path while the user typed a *title`. Same class of "guard tests a path, the
  message talks about titles" confusion, but a different function with a different mechanism:
  `move()` has no sanitisation and no title/filename split at all, since a move never rewrites the
  title. `move()` is also the only path where two fragments with **fully distinct titles** collide,
  and the only one whose own sibling guard already uses the correct word ("filename") one line
  above. Fixing `b99` does not change any behaviour in `move`.
- `fragments-4ht` — `createCollection()` flattens `/` to `-`, so the dialog and `create()`/`move()`
  build different folders for the same name. That is about *destination naming*; this is about the
  *collision guard's* condition and its message.
- No existing issue covers `move`'s collision guard; `br search` for `collection move`,
  `same name` and `dup.md` return 0 issues, and the `move` hits are the unrelated reports listed
  above.

title: useDraft's explicit save() clears pendingDraft and dirty unconditionally (unlike the guarded autosave path), so keystrokes typed while a save is in flight are silently discarded and the app reports 'Fragment saved'

Scratchpad: a new session takes its saved baseline before the previous session's queued write lands, so the reopened buffer shows stale text and the next save fails with a FALSE 'scratchpad changed outside Fragments' conflict
description:
## Summary

A new `useScratchpad` session establishes its `saved` baseline by reading the scratchpad file, but it
does **not** account for a write that the **previous** session already queued to that same path.
The previous session's flush is fire-and-forget (`void library.saveScratchpad(...)` behind a
`pending` chain), so that queued write can land **after** the new session has already read the file.

Two consequences, both user-visible:

1. The reopened session keeps showing the **pre-flush** text, so the scratchpad text the user had
   just typed appears to have vanished - even though it is sitting in the file.
2. Worse, `saved` now disagrees with the file. The user's **next** save passes the stale `expectedBody`
   into `saveScratchpad`, and the real conflict guard in `FragmentLibrary.saveScratchpad` rejects it
   with a false **"The scratchpad changed outside Fragments."** error. Because `useScratchpad` latches
   `conflicted` on any rejection (`fragments-e1h`), one such false conflict then **permanently
   disables scratchpad saving for the rest of the session** - the two bugs compound.

## Affected code

`src/app.tsx` — `useScratchpad`. The session is created in the load effect, which reads the file and
records it as the baseline:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
    const current: ScratchpadSession = {
      path, text: "", saved: "", ready: false, conflicted: false, pending: Promise.resolve(),
    };
    session.current = current;
    setText(""); setStatus("loading");
    let active = true;
    void library.readScratchpad(path).then((loaded) => {
      if (!active) return;
      current.text = loaded;
      current.saved = loaded;      // <-- baseline taken from the file AS IT IS NOW
      current.ready = true;
      setText(loaded); setStatus("saved");
    }).catch(...);
    return () => {
      active = false;
      flush(current);             // <-- queues a write; NOT awaited
      if (session.current === current) session.current = null;
    };
  }, [library, path, flush]);
```

and `flush` never awaits or acknowledges the write it queues:

```ts
current.pending = current.pending
  .then(async () => {
    if (current.conflicted || next === current.saved) return;
    if (session.current === current) setStatus("saving");
    await library.saveScratchpad(current.path, next, current.saved);   // fire and forget
    current.saved = next;
    ...
  })
  .catch((error: Error) => { current.conflicted = true; ... });
```

The guard that then fires the false conflict is in `src/library.ts`:

```ts
await run(() => this.app.vault.process(file, (source) => {
  if (source !== expected) throw new Error("The scratchpad changed outside Fragments. ...");
  return text;
}));
```

Nothing sequences the outgoing session's queued write against the incoming session's read, and
`readScratchpad` is not routed through the same per-path queue that `saveScratchpad` uses
(`FragmentLibrary.queue` is only applied inside `saveScratchpad` itself).

## Trigger

The common case is an ordinary close-and-reopen of the Fragments view:

1. Type into the scratchpad (it starts a 500 ms debounce, and/or blur/Ctrl+S fires a flush).
2. Close the Fragments view before the queued write lands. The cleanup calls `flush(current)`,
   which queues a write to the scratchpad path and does not await it.
3. Reopen the Fragments view. The new session reads the file **before** the queued write is applied.
4. The queued write from step 2 then lands. The session is now showing stale text and holding a
   `saved` value that no longer matches the file.
5. Type anything and save. The stale `expectedBody` is rejected as a false conflict.

An equivalent trigger with no view churn: change the Fragments folder **A -> B -> A** while a
scratchpad edit is pending. Verified separately, same outcome.

## Expected behaviour

Closing and reopening the view should show the scratchpad's persisted text, and a subsequent save
should be validated against what is actually in the file. The outgoing session's pending write is
either awaited before the new session reads, or the new session re-reads after the queue drains.

## Actual behaviour

- The reopened scratchpad shows the **old** text; the user's most recent scratchpad text looks lost.
- The next save fails with a spurious **"The scratchpad changed outside Fragments."** Notice.
- That false failure sets `conflicted = true`, so all later scratchpad saving is dead for the
  session (`fragments-e1h`).

## Reproduction (executed, not reasoned)

`useScratchpad`'s real source (`src/app.tsx:828-915`) was sliced verbatim and run under a
React-accurate effect lifecycle. Harness validation: it independently reproduces both
already-filed scratchpad bugs with the correct symptoms - a reverted edit leaves status `dirty`
(`fragments-tww`) and a rejected write latches `error` while further keystrokes still appear in the
buffer but never save (`fragments-e1h`).

For this bug every vault read and write is a manually-resolved promise keyed by path, so ordering
is exact and **no timer or real scheduler is assumed anywhere**.

```
typed. status: dirty
closed. queued writes: 1 -> target F/s.md
reopened session text: "old" status: saved
land old write -> written
file: "MY IMPORTANT SCRATCH TEXT" | reopened session shows: "old"
>>> EDIT LOOKS LOST TO THE USER? true
next save expectedBody: "old" vs file "MY IMPORTANT SCRATCH TEXT"
land next write -> conflict
>>> FALSE CONFLICT? true | notices: ["scratchpad changed outside Fragments"]
```

Control (the only difference being that the outgoing write lands *before* the reopen reads):

```
land old write -> written
reopened text: "EDIT" status: saved -> consistent
```

The control is clean, which confirms this is specifically the read/queued-write ordering race and
not a general problem with the session design.

## Why this is not a duplicate

- `fragments-e1h` is the one-way `conflicted` latch. It describes what happens *after* a genuine
  conflict. This bead is about a **false** conflict being manufactured in the first place, upstream,
  by the baseline read racing a queued write. (They compound: this bug triggers e1h spuriously.)
- `fragments-tww` is the status label latching after an edit is reverted. Unrelated to session
  lifetimes or to `saved` baselines.
- `fragments-1ft` is a false conflict for **fragments**, from two writes to the same path sharing one
  `expectedBody` snapshot. This is the **scratchpad**, and the stale value comes from a **read** that
  raced an already-queued write - not from reusing a snapshot across two writes. Different function
  (`saveScratchpad` vs `saveBody`), different mechanism, different trigger (view close/reopen or
  folder A->B->A vs two same-path writes), plus a symptom that has no analogue in 1ft at all: the
  reopened buffer displays stale text so the edit appears lost.
- `fragments-07y` is the `createCollection` reserved-name collision that makes the scratchpad path a
  folder. That is how a read can fail; this is about a read that *succeeds* with the wrong value.

## Suggested fix

Sequence the handoff. Either await the outgoing session's `pending` write before the new session
establishes its `saved` baseline, or make the new session re-read once the queue for that path
drains. A minimal version: keep the previous session's `pending` promise reachable and chain the new
session's initial read after it, so the baseline is always taken after the last queued write has
been applied.

title: Scratchpad: a failed read leaves the textarea ENABLED but inert, mislabels the failure as 'Could not save', and silently discards every keystroke/paste for the rest of the session
description:
## Summary

`useScratchpad` has **two different conditions that should gate the scratchpad input, and only one of
them is actually used**. The textarea is disabled based on `status === "loading"`, but whether an
edit is accepted at all is decided by a completely separate flag, `current.ready`.

When the initial `library.readScratchpad(path)` **rejects**, the catch handler sets the status to
`"error"` — but it never sets `current.ready = true`, and it never retries. The result is a
scratchpad that looks alive and is completely dead:

- The header renders `status === "error"` through `scratchpadStatusText`, whose only `"error"`
  string is **"Could not save"** — even though nothing failed to save. Nothing was ever saved,
  because the *load* failed. The user is told the wrong thing about the wrong operation.
- The textarea is **enabled** (`disabled={status === "loading"}` is now false), so it accepts focus
  and looks editable.
- Every keystroke is **silently discarded**: `editScratchpad` returns early on
  `if (!current?.ready) return;` *before* calling `setText`, so React's controlled `<textarea
  value={text}>` immediately reverts the character. No notice, no error, no visible reaction.
- The state is **sticky for the rest of the session**: the read is never retried, so `ready` never
  becomes true. The only escape is changing the Fragments folder or reopening the view.

A user who opens the scratchpad to paste something (its documented purpose) sees an empty editable
box, types or pastes, and the text vanishes with no feedback whatsoever.

## Affected code

`src/app.tsx` — `useScratchpad`, the load effect's error branch:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
    const current: ScratchpadSession = {
      path, text: "", saved: "", ready: false, conflicted: false, pending: Promise.resolve(),
    };
    session.current = current;
    setText(""); setStatus("loading");
    let active = true;
    void library
      .readScratchpad(path)
      .then((loaded) => {
        if (!active) return;
        current.text = loaded;
        current.saved = loaded;
        current.ready = true;      // <-- only set here
        setText(loaded);
        setStatus("saved");
      })
      .catch((error: Error) => {
        if (!active) return;
        setStatus("error");        // <-- status changes, ready stays false, no retry
        errorNotice(error);
      });
    return () => { active = false; flush(current); if (session.current === current) session.current = null; };
  }, [library, path, flush]);
```

versus the edit gate, which uses a different condition entirely:

```ts
const editScratchpad = (value: string): void => {
    const current = session.current;
    if (!current?.ready) return;   // <-- gates ACCEPTANCE, and drops the value
    current.text = value;
    setText(value);
    ...
};
```

and the component's disabled binding, which gates only appearance:

```tsx
<textarea
  className="fragments-scratchpad-editor"
  disabled={status === "loading"}     // <-- a third, different condition
  value={text}
  onChange={(event) => onChange(event.target.value)}
  ... />
```

```ts
const scratchpadStatusText: Record<ScratchpadStatus, string> = {
  loading: "Loading…", dirty: "Unsaved changes", saving: "Saving…", saved: "Saved in vault",
  error: "Could not save",           // <-- one string for BOTH load and save failures
};
```

The net effect is a three-way mismatch: the label, the disabled attribute, and the acceptance gate
all key off different state, so the "error" state is simultaneously "could not save", "not disabled",
and "refuses all input".

## Trigger

Any failure of the initial scratchpad read. `FragmentLibrary.readScratchpad` rejects when the
resolved path is not a `TFile`, and — more commonly — when the underlying `vault.read` throws:

```ts
async readScratchpad(path: string): Promise<string> {
    const file = this.app.vault.getAbstractFileByPath(path);
    if (!file) return "";
    if (!(file instanceof TFile)) throw new Error("The scratchpad path is not a Markdown file.");
    return run(() => this.app.vault.read(file));
}
```

Reachable, non-exotic routes to that rejection, none of which require the user to have done anything
unusual:

1. **The scratchpad file is removed or renamed while the view is open** (sync client, another
   device, a filesystem watcher, or the user deleting it in Obsidian). The path lookup succeeds, the
   read then fails.
2. **Any transient `vault.read` error** — file locked, permission problem, or an I/O error. Note
   that `run()` wraps the operation in `Effect.tryPromise`, which per `fragments-tmf` replaces the
   real message with a generic one, so the user gets
   `"An unknown error occurred in Effect.tryPromise"` and no actionable detail.
3. The path resolving to a directory (the `fragments-07y` scenario) — that is one *cause* of a read
   rejection, but see the relationship note below.

Once the read has failed, the scratchpad is inert until the Fragments folder changes or the view is
reopened.

## Expected behaviour

Either (a) a read failure should leave the scratchpad **disabled and honestly labelled** (for
example "Could not load scratchpad"), so the user is not invited to type into a dead box; or
(b) the session should still accept input and save it, treating the read failure as non-fatal — the
user's pasted text should not be thrown away because a load failed. Retrying the read is a third
option. What should not happen is a control that appears editable, reports the wrong failure, and
discards input without a trace.

## Actual behaviour

- Header: **"Could not save"** (wrong operation named).
- Textarea: **enabled**, focused on click, and every keystroke/paste is reverted with no message.
- `saveScratchpad` is never called — 0 write attempts.
- The state persists for the session; the read is not retried.

## Reproduction (executed, not reasoned)

`useScratchpad`'s real source (`src/app.tsx:828-915`) was sliced verbatim and executed under a
React-accurate effect lifecycle. Harness validation: it independently reproduces both already-filed
scratchpad bugs with the correct symptoms before any new result is trusted — a reverted edit leaves
status `"dirty"` (`fragments-tww`), and a rejected write latches `"error"` while further keystrokes
still appear in the buffer but never save (`fragments-e1h`).

The scratchpad read here is a manually-resolved promise, so no scheduler is assumed.

```
status after read failure : error -> header shows: "Could not save"
textarea disabled?        : false (disabled only when status==='loading')
text shown                : ""
notices                   : ["An unknown error occurred in Effect.tryPromise"]

user types 'my-pasted-secret':
  text after editScratchpad: ""   <-- React reverts: input silently discarded
  status                   : error
  any save attempted?      : NO - saveScratchpad never called
  any notice explaining?   : 1

does it recover without changing path / reopening?
  second attempt text       : "" | saves: 0
```

The single Notice shown is the generic read error; nothing tells the user their input is being
dropped.

## Relationship to existing beads (stated up front)

- `fragments-07y` is a **cause** of one way to reach a read rejection (a collection named
  `_fragments-scratchpad.md` turns the scratchpad path into a folder). It is filed against
  `FragmentLibrary.createCollection` and its stated impact is that "both its read and its write
  throw". This bead is filed against **`useScratchpad`'s response** to a read rejection and is
  reachable by other causes (file deleted/renamed mid-session, transient `vault.read` failure). If
  the team prefers a single issue, the two are worth merging, but only 07y's is fixed by adding a
  reserved-name guard in `createCollection`; this one is not.
- `fragments-e1h` is the write-side one-way `conflicted` latch, i.e. what happens *after* a genuine
  save failure. This is the **load**-side path, and it never even reaches a save.
- `fragments-tmf` is the swallowed error message from `run()`. That makes the symptom harder to
  diagnose but is a separate defect in a different function.
- `fragments-scratchpad-new-session-baseline-races-queued-wri-i41` is the queued-write/baseline
  ordering race. Different failure mode: that one is a *successful* read with a stale value; this one
  is a *failed* read.

## Suggested fix

Make the three conditions one. Either key the textarea's `disabled` and the label off the same
`ready`/`status` state the edit gate uses, and give load and save failures distinct labels (for
example `"Could not load scratchpad"` vs `"Could not save"`); and/or treat a failed read as
non-fatal by setting `ready = true` with an empty baseline so the user can still type and have it
persisted, plus retry the read once.

title: An active list tag filter survives with no chip representing it, so the list empties to 'No fragments found' while the library is still full
description:
## Summary `tagFilter` is controller state that is applied to the list **independently of the chip row that represents it**. The chip row is rendered from a *truncated, recomputed* slice of the tag counts, and `tagFilter` is never reconciled with it or cleared when its tag disappears. So an active tag filter can end up with **no visible control at all** — and because `filtered` is then empty, the list renders its **"No fragments found. Create a fragment"** empty state while the user's library is in fact full. The UI actively tells the user their snippets do not exist. The minimal way to reach this is not exotic: filter by a tag, then remove that tag from the fragment using the plugin's own `+ tag` editor. The filter survives, the chip disappears, and the list empties. ## Affected code `src/app.tsx` — the filter is raw state in `useController`: ```ts const [tagFilter, setTagFilter] = useState(""); ``` `searchFragments` applies it as a hard predicate (`src/search.ts`): ```ts if (tagFilter && !entry.fragment.tags.includes(tagFilter)) continue; ``` but the chip row is derived from a **freshly recomputed, truncated** list (`src/app.tsx`, `ListPane`): ```tsx {tags.slice(0, 5).map(([tag]) => ( ))} ``` where `tags = useMemo(() => countTags(entries), [entries])` and `countTags` returns only the top **20** tags, of which the row shows the first **5**. Three independent gaps follow: 1. **The tag stops existing.** When the last fragment carrying the filtered tag loses it, the tag vanishes from `countTags`, so its chip is no longer rendered — while `tagFilter` still holds its value. 2. **The tag is merely outranked.** Even if it still exists, a new tag with a higher count displaces it from `slice(0, 5)` and its chip is not rendered. 3. **The `All` chip is not a fallback indicator.** It is highlighted only when `tagFilter` is falsy (`className={!tagFilter ? "active" : ""}`), so while a stale filter is active the `All` chip is *also* inactive. The result is **zero** highlighted chips. `selectScope` and `createFragment` both reset `tagFilter`, but every other path that re-derives `entries` — a tag edit, an autosave re-index, a `library.load()`, a vault event — leaves it set. `ListPane` then renders the misleading empty state purely from `filtered.length`: ```tsx {filtered.length ? () : (
No fragments found.
)} ``` ## Trigger 1. Filter the list with a tag chip (e.g. click `#work`). 2. While that filter is active, edit the only fragment carrying `#work` with the **`+ tag`** editor and remove the tag. 3. The list empties and reports that no fragments were found. ## Impact - **The UI states a falsehood.** The library still contains the fragments — the probe reports `2` Markdown files in the vault — yet the list says "No fragments found" and offers to create one. A user who trusts it will create a duplicate snippet. - **The active filter is invisible.** No chip is highlighted: the filtered tag's chip is gone and `All` is inactive precisely *because* the filter is set. There is no on-screen explanation for the empty result set. - **Recovery is non-obvious.** The only way out is the undifferentiated `All` button, which is not highlighted and not labelled as "clear the active filter". - **The same state is reachable by rank alone** (the tag still exists but drops out of the top 5), so a user who merely edits tags on a few fragments can end up in a filtered state with no representation. - It is easy to mistake for data loss, which is the worst possible diagnosis: the files are intact and the plugin is only misreporting. ## Reproduction (deterministic) Mounts the **real** `AppShell` (React 19 + the repository's own `src/app.tsx`) in jsdom against an in-memory Obsidian vault, and drives the **real** `+ tag` editor through DOM events. Only the vault, the Obsidian API and the DOM are doubles; the plugin, view, React tree, controller and search code are the repository's own code bundled from `src/`. Vault: `Fragments/a.md` (`tags: ["work"]`), `Fragments/b.md` (`tags: ["home"]`). ```js // 1. filter by the #work chip document.querySelector(".fragments-filter-row button#work").click(); // 2. open the in-app tag editor on the selected fragment and clear the tag click(".fragments-tags button"); // "+ tag" setValue(".fragments-tag-input", ""); dispatch(".fragments-tag-input", "focusout"); // React onBlur ``` Observed: ``` === STATE 1: pristine === chips : ["All*","#work","#home"] rows : 2 empty state : null sidebar tags : ["#work","#home"] === STATE 2: user filters by #work (the list chip) === chips : ["All","#work*","#home"] rows : 1 empty state : null === STATE 3: user edits Alpha's tags and REMOVES #work (in-app '+ tag' editor) === tag editor value : "work" chips : ["All","#home"] <-- the #work chip is GONE rows : 0 empty state : "No fragments found.Create a fragment" sidebar tags : ["#home"] === VERDICT === vault fragments still exist : 2 rows shown : 0 any chip indicates a filter : false <-- not even "All" empty state claims : "No fragments found.Create a fragment" notices : [] => filtered-to-zero, no indicator, claims 'no fragments found': true ``` The rank-only variant was reproduced the same way, by retagging five fragments onto a new tag so the filtered tag left the top 5: ``` chips after library chg: [{"text":"All","active":false},{"text":"#hot","active":false},{"text":"#tag6","active":false}] rows after library chg : 0 any chip highlighted? : false ``` ## Expected vs actual - **Expected:** the chip row always represents the filters that are actually applied. Either an active tag filter keeps a visible highlighted chip, or the filter is dropped when its tag is removed/displaced. And when `filtered` is empty the list must not claim the library is empty if entries exist. - **Actual:** the filter survives silently with zero representation, and the empty state asserts "No fragments found" for a library that still holds every fragment. ## Suggested fix Reconcile the filter with the chips that are actually rendered, and make the empty state honest. Cheapest correct fix — drop a filter whose tag no longer exists, in the same place the counts are derived: ```tsx const tags = useMemo(() => countTags(entries), [entries]); // a filter whose tag vanished (or fell out of the rendered row) must not stay applied useEffect(() => { if (tagFilter && !tags.some(([tag]) => tag === tagFilter)) setTagFilter(""); }, [tagFilter, tags]); ``` Two supporting changes are worth making at the same time: - Render the active tag as a chip **even if it is outside `tags.slice(0, 5)`** (or render the filter row from the union of the top 5 and the active filter), so an applied filter is always visible and always clearable. - Make the empty state distinguish "nothing matches the current filter" from "the library is empty", e.g. surface the active scope/filter in the message and offer "Clear filter" next to "Create a fragment". ## Relationship to other reports - `fragments-lex` (tag case normalisation) and `fragments-rt7` (scalar tag splitting) are tag *parsing* defects in `src/library.ts`; `fragments-5ir` is tag *de-duplication*. None of them concerns how the list pane's filter controls are rendered or how `tagFilter` is reconciled. - `fragments-virtuallist-stale-scrolltop-empty-window-w72` also mentions the "No fragments found" string, but as the thing its (empty-render) bug is *not*; that issue is about scroll offsets, not about filters or the empty state's claims. - `fragments-palette-pick-overridden-by-active-scope-gp9` is about the *command palette* ignoring the active scope; this is the opposite direction — a filter that is applied with no way to see it. - `br search` for "filter chip", "stale filter", "top 5 tags", "slice(0, 5)" and "filter indicator" return 0 issues.

title: Scratchpad status latches on 'Unsaved changes' after an edit is reverted: flush's early return skips setStatus, and Ctrl+S is then a no-op that cannot clear the wrong label
description:
## Summary

`useScratchpad`'s `flush` short-circuits the whole save pipeline when the pending text already
equals the last-saved text:

```ts
if (current.conflicted || next === current.saved) return;
```

That `return` skips **both** the write and the `setStatus(...)` that would otherwise report the
result. So when the user edits the scratchpad and then returns the text to its saved value, the
status indicator is left in the `dirty` state it was set to by `editScratchpad`, and it stays
there for the rest of the session.

The scratchpad header then permanently claims **"Unsaved changes"** for a scratchpad that has
nothing unsaved, and the documented save action cannot clear it: Ctrl+S (and blur-on-save) both
call `flush`, which hits the same `next === current.saved` early return, writes nothing, and
reports nothing. The indicator is only corrected by making a *new* edit that actually persists.

This is an asymmetry with the fragment editor, which has no such early return and correctly
settles back to `Saved` — see the trace below.

## Trigger

Open the scratchpad, change its text, then change it back to exactly what the file contains,
before the 500 ms debounce elapses (a backspace, an undo, or dragging a selection away).
`editScratchpad` sets `status = "dirty"` and re-arms the timer on every keystroke, so the reverted
text reaches `flush` with `next === current.saved`.

## Affected code

`src/app.tsx` — `useScratchpad`

```ts
const flush = useCallback((current: ScratchpadSession) => {
    if (current.timer !== undefined) window.clearTimeout(current.timer);
    current.timer = undefined;
    if (!current.ready || current.conflicted) return;
    const next = current.text;
    current.pending = current.pending
      .then(async () => {
        if (current.conflicted || next === current.saved) return;   // <-- no setStatus on this path
        if (session.current === current) setStatus("saving");
        await library.saveScratchpad(current.path, next, current.saved);
        current.saved = next;
        if (session.current === current)
          setStatus(current.text === current.saved ? "saved" : "dirty");
      })
      ...
```

`editScratchpad` is the only other writer of `dirty`:

```ts
setStatus("dirty");
if (current.timer !== undefined) window.clearTimeout(current.timer);
current.timer = window.setTimeout(() => flush(current), 500);
```

## Observed vs expected

Trace, starting from a scratchpad whose file contains `"notes"` (`current.saved === "notes"`,
`current.text === "notes"`, `status === "saved"`):

| step | user action | `current.text` | `status` after | file |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | type `x` | `"notesx"` | `dirty` (set by `editScratchpad`) | `"notes"` |
| 2 | backspace (< 500 ms) | `"notes"` | `dirty` (timer re-armed) | `"notes"` |
| 3 | debounce fires | `"notes"` | **`dirty`** — early return, no `setStatus` | `"notes"` |

Expected: step 3 reports `saved`, matching the fragment editor's behaviour for the identical
edit-then-revert sequence (`useDraft` has no `next === saved` early return; it always settles
through `setDirty(false)`), and Ctrl+S afterwards is a harmless no-op that leaves the label
truthful.

## Reproduction

In the app:

1. Open Fragments with a fragment selected and show the scratchpad.
2. Type a character — the header flips to **"Unsaved changes"**.
3. Delete it again (or press Ctrl+Z) within half a second, so the text matches the file again.
4. Wait for the debounce. The header still reads **"Unsaved changes"**.
5. Press Ctrl+S in the scratchpad. Nothing is written and the label does not change.

The scratchpad file is byte-identical to the vault throughout steps 3-5, so the label is
demonstrably wrong.

## Not a duplicate

- `fragments-e1h` — also latches scratchpad state, but on the one-way `conflicted` flag set by a
  failed write. Here no write is attempted, no error occurs, `conflicted` stays `false`, and
  saving continues to work; only the reported status is stuck.
- `fragments-w3w` — the fragment editor's false **"Saved"**; opposite polarity and a different
  hook (`useDraft`).
- `fragments-07y` — `createCollection()` creating a folder at the scratchpad path.

## Acceptance criteria

- After an edit that returns the text to its last-saved value, the scratchpad header reports
  `saved`, and Ctrl+S leaves the label truthful.
- The early return still avoids a redundant vault write when the text is unchanged.
- A genuinely unsaved scratchpad continues to report `Unsaved changes` and to persist.

title: useDraft does not reset body on a fragment switch, so autosave validates the new fragment against the previous fragment's text and rejects the write forever
description:
## Summary

`useDraft` clears `body`/`draft` **only** in its `if (!selected)` branch. On a normal
fragment switch **A -> B** it leaves `body` holding fragment A's last-saved text for the
entire in-flight window of `library.read(B)`.

The 700 ms autosave effect passes `body` as the `expectedBody` argument to
`library.saveBody(selected, draft, body)`. So during that window a save aimed at **B** is
validated against **A's** content, `FragmentLibrary.saveBody`'s conflict check fails, and the
write is rejected. The state is never repaired, so **every subsequent autosave fails the same
way forever**.

## Affected code

- `src/app.tsx` `useDraft`, load effect (lines ~112-134) - resets `body`/`draft` only when
  `selected` is null:
  ```ts
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!selected) { setBody(""); setDraft(""); return undefined; }   // <- only null
    let active = true;
    void library.read(selected).then((text) => { /* sets body/draft on resolve */ });
  }, [selected, modified, library]);
  ```
  There is no `else` branch that clears `body` for a *changed* selection, so between the
  `setSelected(B)` render and the resolution of `read(B)`, `body` is still A's text.
- `src/app.tsx` `useDraft`, autosave effect - consumes the stale `body` as the snapshot:
  ```ts
  void library.saveBody(selected, draft, body)   // selected = B, body = A's text
  ```
- `src/library.ts` `FragmentLibrary.saveBody` - the check that rejects the write:
  ```ts
  if (expectedBody !== undefined && bodyOf(source) !== expectedBody) {
    throw new Error("This note changed outside Fragments. ...");
  }
  ```

## Trigger

1. Open fragment A in Fragments, let it load.
2. Type in A (optional; the bug fires either way, this just makes A's state non-empty).
3. Click fragment B in the list. `read(B)` starts and has **not** resolved yet.
4. Start typing in B before B's content finishes loading. This is the ordinary case: clicking a
   row focuses the editor immediately, and `library.read` is a real async vault read
   (`cachedRead`), so the window is genuinely reachable.
5. Stop typing for 700 ms.

## Expected behaviour

Typing in B autosaves B, validated against B's own last-saved body.

## Actual behaviour

- A spurious **"This note changed outside Fragments. Copy your draft, then reopen the note
  before saving."** Notice is shown.
- **B's keystrokes are never written to disk.**
- `dirty` stays `true` and `body` stays A's text, so every subsequent autosave retries and
  fails identically. The failure is **permanent**, not transient.
- Secondary symptom: while B is loading, the editor still renders **A's text**, so the wrong
  fragment's content is briefly displayed for the newly selected fragment.

Measured: 7 save attempts across ~4 s of continued typing, **all rejected**, 6 Notices, B's
file byte-identical to its original. A's own draft is flushed correctly first (the unmount
flush effect saves A properly), which isolates the failure to the B write.

## Reproduction (executed, not reasoned)

`useDraft`'s real source (`src/app.tsx:104-191`) was sliced verbatim into a module and
executed under a React-accurate effect lifecycle: cleanups and effects run in definition
order on every dep change, effect closures capture the values from the render that created
them, timers are a controllable fake, and `saveBody` is a stub mirroring
`FragmentLibrary.saveBody`'s `expectedBody` guard verbatim.

Observed call sequence (the defective one is the second):

```
{"path":"Fragments/A.md","body":"AAA original + typed","expectedBody":"AAA original"}   <- correct flush of A
{"path":"Fragments/B.md","body":"BBB original + typed","expectedBody":"AAA original"}   <- expectedBody is A's
```

`expectedBody` for the write to B is `"AAA original"` - fragment A's body.

State during the window, straight from the harness:

```
right after click on B    body="AAA original"   draft="AAA original + typed"    dirty=true
after typing in B         body="AAA original"   draft="BBB original + typed"    dirty=true
```

`body` never leaves A's value, which is the root cause.

## Harness caveat, stated for honesty

An earlier revision of the harness had a defect **in the harness itself**: the effect store
replaced each effect object on every render without carrying the previous `cleanup` forward,
so cleanups silently never ran. That was caught and fixed before filing. All figures above
come from the corrected runtime, in which A's unmount-flush runs and correctly saves A first
- so the B failure is not an artifact of a missing flush. The bug is in `useDraft`, not in
the harness.

## Why this is not a duplicate

- `fragments-1ft`: two writes to the **same** path queued with the **same** `expectedBody`
  snapshot. This bug writes to a **different** path carrying the **previous fragment's**
  `expectedBody`. Root cause is state that is never reset on a selection change, not a
  missing re-read of the snapshot before a queued write.
- `fragments-nzo`: the selection is **nulled**. Here the selection *changes* A -> B and
  `body`/`draft` are not cleared at all.
- `fragments-w3w`: the load effect's freshness test reads a **stale `dirty` closure**. This
  failure does not depend on the `dirty` closure at all.
- `fragments-tot`: the explicit `save()` clears `pendingDraft`/`dirty` unconditionally while
  a save is in flight. Different trigger and different mechanism.

## Suggested fix

Clear the draft state when the selection **changes**, not only when it becomes null - e.g.
track the previously loaded path in `loadedPath.current` and reset `body` (and the editor
buffer) when `selected !== loadedPath.current`, or pass the `expectedBody` for the path being
written rather than reusing a cross-fragment `body`.

fragments-copy-clips-previous-fragment-body-during-read-wi-99b (CrimsonOtter). Both trace to the

should probably fix them together:

  recoverable, no data loss).
- THIS bead covers the `body` half, observed through the 700ms autosave ->
  `library.saveBody(selected, draft, body)` -> `expectedBody` is the previous fragment's text ->
  FragmentLibrary.saveBody's guard rejects the write. Unlike 99b this is NOT recoverable from the
  UI: `dirty` stays true, every subsequent autosave fails identically, the user sees a spurious

title: The 'Name' sort is silently overridden by relevance scoring, so the sort toggle is inert and misreports the ordering whenever a query is active
description:
The "Name" sort control is silently overridden by relevance scoring: as soon as a search query is active, the list is ordered by score, not by name, and the toggle frequently produces an order identical to "Recent".

## Root cause

`src/search.ts`, `compare`:

```ts
function compare(left: RankedFragment, right: RankedFragment, sort: "recent" | "name"): number {
  if (left.score !== right.score) return right.score - left.score;
  return sort === "name"
    ? left.fragment.title.localeCompare(right.fragment.title)
    : right.fragment.modified - left.fragment.modified;
}
```

Score is the **primary** key for both sort modes; `sort` only selects the **tie-break**. So `sort: "name"` can never reorder two fragments whose scores differ.

The list header exposes this as a two-state toggle in `src/app.tsx`:

```jsx
<button onClick={() => setSort(sort === "recent" ? "name" : "recent")}>
  {sort === "recent" ? "Recent" : "Name"} <ChevronDown size={11} />
</button>
```

The button renders the active mode, so when it reads "Name" the list is contractually alphabetical. It is not.

## Trigger

1. Open Fragments, leave the sort control on "Recent".
2. Type any query into the list search field that does not match every fragment equally (e.g. `m`, when one fragment is titled `Mango` and another is titled `Zebra`).
3. Click the sort button so it reads **"Name"**.

The list does not become alphabetical, and in many cases does not change at all.

This also explains why the control appears to work normally until you search: with an **empty** query every fragment scores 0 (see the `terms` loop in `entryScore`), all scores tie, and `compare` falls through to the name tie-break — so "Name" is genuinely alphabetical until the first keystroke, then silently stops being.

## Impact

- The user explicitly asks for alphabetical order, the UI confirms it is in "Name" mode, and gets relevance order. There is no indicator that the ordering is being overridden.
- In the cases where every result has a distinct score, clicking the toggle produces a **byte-identical** list, so the control reads as completely inert.
- It is silent: no notice, no disabled state, no tooltip explaining that search results are always relevance-ordered.

## Affected code

- `src/search.ts` — `compare` (root cause: score is the primary key regardless of `sort`).
- `src/app.tsx` — `useController` `sort` state and the header sort toggle in `ListPane`; also `GlobalSearch`, which passes no `sort` and therefore always uses the `"recent"` tie-break.

## Reproduction (deterministic, real code)

Executed the **real production `src/search.ts`**, bundled with esbuild (`src/search.ts --bundle --format=esm`). The bundle has zero runtime imports because `./library` is a type-only import, so no stub or test double is involved. Fixtures use the same shape `FragmentLibrary.fragmentFrom` produces, including the lowercased `searchText` that `includeBody` matching reads.

```
fixtures: Zebra(body "aardvark")   Apple(body "a")   Mango(body "")

query=""
  sort:"recent" -> ["Zebra","Apple","Mango"]
  sort:"name"   -> ["Apple","Mango","Zebra"]   orders identical: false
  name order is alphabetical: true            <-- correct, because all scores tie at 0

query="a"
  sort:"recent" -> ["Apple","Mango","Zebra"]
  sort:"name"   -> ["Apple","Mango","Zebra"]   orders identical: true   <-- toggle is a NO-OP
```

Swept 50 term/modified combinations. Across them:

- the sort toggle returned an **identical order in 20/50** cases;
- `"name"` mode returned a **non-alphabetical order in 30/50** cases.

Concrete non-alphabetical case, query `m`, all three bodies matching so all three are results:

```
Mango   title matches "m" at 0  -> 100 - 4/4 = 99, +8 title bonus = 107
Apple   title matches "m" at 2  -> 72 - 0.2 = 71.8, +8            =  79.8
Zebra   no "m" in title        -> fieldScore -1, body fallback   =  15

sort:"name" -> ["Mango","Apple","Zebra"]
```

`"Mango","Apple","Zebra"` is not alphabetical, even though the control is in "Name" mode.

## Expected vs actual

- **Expected:** in "Name" mode the list is ordered by title, with relevance only as a tie-break (or the control is hidden/disabled while a query is active, with the reason surfaced).
- **Actual:** the list is always ordered by relevance score first. "Name" mode is alphabetical only while the query is empty, and is otherwise frequently identical to "Recent".

## Suggested fix

Make the selected sort mode the primary key in `compare` and demote score to the tie-break, e.g. for `sort === "name"` compare `title.localeCompare` first and use score only when titles tie. If relevance-first ordering is genuinely wanted for search results, then the control should not present itself as a sort mode in that state — surface it (disable the button, or label the results "by relevance") so it does not claim an ordering it is not applying.

## Relationship to existing issues

I checked the full corpus. No existing bead concerns result *ordering* or the sort control; the `sort`/`relevance` keyword hits in other beads are incidental occurrences of `Array.prototype.sort` in unrelated code samples.

- `fragments-jp2` is the closest by keyword (`fieldScore`/relevance) but a different function and opposite failure: jp2 is a score going *negative* so a real match is *dropped*; this is scores being *correct but dominant* so the ordering is wrong. I fuzzed 40,000 trials against a substring oracle and found zero dropped real matches at normal lengths, which confirms jp2 is confined to >720-character fields and does not cover ordering.
- Not a tag defect (`lex`, `rt7`, `5ir`): the decisive fixture has no tags at all.
- Not the palette's presentation (`ijg`, `gp9`): those concern which entries the palette lists and which fragment a pick opens, not the order of the list produced by `searchFragments`.
- Independent of `fragments-nnn` (bare `#` degenerating to an empty query): that report is about *which* fragments match, this is about the *order* of those that do. The empty-query case is the one case where this bug does not appear, which is exactly why they are separate.

## Evidence quality

Observed by executing the real module. `indexFragments`/`searchFragments` are pure and exported, so the only inputs are plain data objects and no test double or behavioural assumption is involved. The `app.tsx` toggle and the `GlobalSearch` call site were read from source, not executed.
